newsitem.title: USA: Perot lashes out at debate exclusion.
newsitem.headline: Perot lashes out at debate exclusion.

text.p: Reform Party presidential nominee Ross Perot on Tuesday lashed out at the decision to exclude him from the campaign debates and threatened to expose the Debates Commission as "corrupt" and manipulative.

Lawyers for Perot and his running mate, economist Pat Choate, filed papers in U.S. District Court in Washington on Monday seeking an injunction to force their inclusion in presidential and vice presidential debates next month.

The Texas billionaire, in an interview on PBS' NewsHour with Jim Lehrer, said the commission did not even talk to anyone from the Reform Party before making its decision and claimed he was excluded based on the "subjective criteria" of five Democrats and five Republicans.
Perot said the commission was controlled by special interests and promised to name them in a few days.

"The American people don't even know that this is a private corporation, funded privately and they don't know that this organisation won't even tell you who funds it. We'll get that in a few days and we'll tell you and you're going to see some really big special interests," he said.
"We're going to pull this little skunk up by the tail and let the American people see how the system is being manipulated," Perot declared.

Negotiators for President Bill Clinton and Republican candidate Bob Dole agreed to hold two one-on-one televised presidential debates between their candidates on Oct 6 in Hartford, Connecticut, and Oct. 16 in San Diego. A vice presidential debate was scheduled for Oct. 9 in St. Petersburg, Florida.
Clinton originally backed Perot's demand to participate, while Dole opposed it.

The Perot camp has portrayed the move as an establishment effort to smother a third-party candidate who won 19 percent of the popular vote in the 1992 presidential election after making a strong mark in that year's debates.

"The establishment didn't want us to have a voice because they want to protect the two-party system and because they do not want a third party under any circumstances, so they froze us out," Perot said.

Perot's lawsuit named the Federal Election Commission, which oversees campaign financing laws but has not been involved in debate preparations, as the agency that should be directed to have the Reform Party candidates included. The suit argues that the debate commission, established by the two major parties in the 1980s, is a fraudulent entity.

His lawyers said they hoped a judge would hold a hearing this week. They would argue that Perot's constitutional rights were violated when the commission decided he should not be included because he had no chance of being elected.

Perot told PBS the debate commission was "corrupt" and said when he uncovered the names of those funding it, "you're going to see the same people and the same special interests who give a lot of money and get a huge return for their contributions."
